conceptTag: A growth hack that might be a dark pattern
readerTitle: Four growth hacks, one question: would customers thank you?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (B2B 청소·사무용품 유통사의 주문 사이트와 청소 서비스 계약) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 다크 패턴 용어의 유래만 실제 사실
insight: 성장 아이디어는 고객이 그 장치를 알아챈 뒤에도 여전히 통하는지로 판단한다. 알아채는 순간 통하지 않으면 다크 패턴이다.
misconception: 단기 테스트에서 매출이 오르고 약관에 적혀 있기만 하면 공정한 성장 전략이다.

sources.text: Harry Brignull, deceptive.design (구 darkpatterns.org). 2010년에 'dark patterns' 용어를 제안
회사, 컨설턴트, 18% 수치 등 모든 시나리오는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Harry Brignull이 2010년에 'dark patterns'라는 용어를 만들었다는 내용은 게시 전 deceptive.design 사이트에서 다시 확인하세요.
'2주 만에 주문 18% 증가', '60일 전 서면 해지', '30일 전 알림' 등은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 연구 결과처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
자동 갱신·해지 관련 법규는 국가마다 다르고 자주 바뀝니다. 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 카드에서 특정 법규는 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The consultant's slide said +18% in two weeks.
body: You run Brightline, a regional supplier of cleaning and office supplies for small businesses. Clinics, offices and gyms order through your website. Many also hire your cleaning crews on yearly contracts.
A growth consultant brings four ideas. Each one would lift your sales numbers. Each one might also be a trick.

image.label: A consultant presenting a rising sales chart to a small business owner
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고 사무실에서 컨설턴트가 '+18%' 상승 그래프 슬라이드를 가리키고, 사업주는 뒤편 선반의 청소용품 상자를 바라보며 고민하는 장면. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Idea 1: tick the auto-reorder box for them.
body: At checkout, the consultant wants "Reorder this every month" ticked by default. Most buyers won't notice, so repeat orders will jump.

options.text: Keep it pre-ticked. Customers can always untick it
options.feedback: Repeat orders rise, but many are orders nobody meant to place. You pay for the returns, the refunds and the angry calls from office managers.
Nobody gets tricked, but you lose a real convenience. Plenty of offices would love never to run out of paper towels.

options.text: Offer it unticked, show the next delivery date, and email a reminder before each shipment
options.feedback: Fewer sign-ups than the pre-ticked box, but each one is a customer who chose it. Those customers tend to stay.

cards.title: Idea 2: "Only 3 left!" on every product.
body: Say you chose the clear, opt-in reorder. Next, the consultant wants a low-stock warning on every item, true or not. Your warehouse holds weeks of stock for most items.

options.text: Show it everywhere. It's just marketing
options.feedback: Buyers order more today. But an office manager who sees "3 left" for a month learns your labels lie, and then ignores the real warnings.

options.text: Show real stock levels, and warn only when stock is actually low
options.feedback: You keep urgency where it's true, which is when it helps buyers plan. Honest scarcity is information. Fake scarcity is pressure.
Safe, but buyers lose something useful. A clinic that knows gloves are running short can order early.

cards.title: Idea 3: let the cleaning contracts renew quietly.
body: Say you chose honest stock labels. Your cleaning contracts renew each year unless the client cancels in writing 60 days ahead.
The consultant says: stop sending renewal reminders. Fewer clients will remember to cancel.

options.text: Stop the reminders. The terms are in the contract
options.feedback: Renewals rise this year. But a client surprised by an unwanted bill feels trapped, and trapped clients leave loudly when they finally can.

options.text: Send a clear reminder before the cancel deadline, and let clients cancel online
options.feedback: A few more clients leave. The ones who stay chose to, so your renewal rate now tells you something real about your service.

options.text: Drop auto-renewal and make every client re-sign each year
options.feedback: Very fair, but happy clients face paperwork and some lapse by accident. Auto-renewal isn't the problem. Hiding it is.

cards.title: Idea 4: judge it by the two-week test.
body: Say you chose the reminder. The consultant's last pitch: his test lifted orders 18% in two weeks, so roll everything out. How should you judge a change like this?

options.text: Trust it. 18% is a big, clear lift
options.feedback: Two weeks shows who clicked, not who regretted it. Returns, refunds and cancellations arrive later.

options.text: Track it for three months: repeat orders, returns, complaints and renewals
options.feedback: Slower, but it measures what the change does to customers, not just to one fortnight of sales.

options.text: Skip testing and go by gut
options.feedback: Your gut may be right about the tricks, but you'll never know which honest changes actually help.

cards.title: Would it still work if they understood it?
body: A **dark pattern** is a design that gets people to do something they didn't mean to do: buy more, sign up, or stay. UX designer Harry Brignull coined the term in 2010.
A simple check: explain the tactic to the customer out loud. An honest nudge still works, because it helps them do what they wanted. A dark pattern **stops working the moment they see it**.

image.label: Two doors: one labeled clearly, one hidden behind a curtain
image.brief: 두 가지 장치를 나란히 비교하는 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 'Explained out loud → still works' 라벨과 밝은 문, 오른쪽은 'Explained out loud → stops working' 라벨과 커튼 뒤에 숨은 문. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Not every bit of friction is a trick.
body: A confirmation step before a large order is friction that protects the buyer. Urgency is fine when it's true. A default is fine when most customers would pick it anyway.
And honest design doesn't guarantee growth. Every change, fair or not, still needs measuring over the time it takes customers to react.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the same tricks appear as pre-ticked add-ons, free trials that start charging without warning, and cancel buttons hidden behind a support chat. The test is the same: would it survive being explained?

cards.title: Growth that only works when customers don't notice is borrowed.
body: Each decision used an idea from this unit:
list: **Opt-in reorder:** a nudge that helps, not a hidden default
**Honest stock labels:** persuasion uses true information, manipulation doesn't
**Renewal reminders:** make leaving as clear as staying
**Three-month tracking:** a quick test result isn't the real-world effect
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick one thing on your checkout, invoice or contract that lifts sales. Explain it out loud as if to a customer. Would it still work?
